title: repo-inventory view silently drops every listing entry without a dot or slash
description:
The repo-inventory view SILENTLY DISCARDS every output line that does not look like a file path. Entries are not counted, not sampled, and not mentioned anywhere. The agent sees a confident, well-formed inventory block that is simply missing most of the listing.

REPRODUCTION (live origin/main binary, TokenZero 78a9a12):

  mkdir -p /tmp/az/inv/alpha /tmp/az/inv/beta /tmp/az/inv/gamma
  touch /tmp/az/inv/notes.txt
  zero.token.shell("ls /tmp/az/inv; ls /tmp/az/DOES_NOT_EXIST")

Actual visible output:

  repo_inventory:
  command: ls /tmp/az/inv; ls /tmp/az/DOES_NOT_EXIST
  files_seen: 1
  dirs_seen: 0
  sample_paths:
  - notes.txt
  exit: 1

alpha, beta and gamma are GONE. Not in sample_paths, not in dirs_seen, not in
files_seen, not reflected in any count. Three of the four entries in the
directory vanished, and nothing in the output hints that anything was dropped.
There is no truncation marker because the renderer does not believe it
truncated anything.

I hit this for real before reducing it: "ls ~/AI/pi; ls ~/.pi; ls ~/.pi/extensions"
returned a single sample_paths entry, agent.bak-clean-20260721-185218, because
that was the only name in the whole combined listing containing a dot. I
concluded the extensions directory was empty. It is not.

ROOT CAUSE

crates/tokenzero-core/src/render/domain.rs, inventory_stats:

  for line in output.lines().map(str::trim) {
      if line.is_empty() || starts_with("===") || starts_with("---") { continue; }
      if line.ends_with('/') {
          stats.dirs += 1;
      } else if is_file(line) {
          stats.files += 1;
          if stats.paths.len() < sample_limit { stats.paths.push(line); }
      }
      ...
  }

There is no else. A line that neither ends in '/' nor satisfies is_file falls
through both arms and is dropped without a trace.

The predicate passed by repo_inventory_view is

  |line| line.contains('/') || line.contains('.')

so for the extremely common case of a bare "ls dir" (no -la, no trailing
slashes, relative names), ANY entry without a dot in its name is discarded.
That is most directory names in most repos: src, crates, target, docs, scripts.
Plain files without extensions are lost too: README, Makefile, LICENSE.

The compact path has the same shape. render/noise.rs compact_repo_inventory_view
calls inventory_stats with looks_like_inventory_file_path, which requires a
slash, a backslash, or a dot in the basename, so it drops dotless entries in
exactly the same way. Both entry points are affected.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE USUAL ELISION

Every other lossy surface in TokenZero announces itself: a ref, a lossy footer,
an "omitted N lines" marker. This one does not. files_seen: 1 is a positive
factual claim about the listing, and it is wrong. An agent has no reason to
double-check a count that the renderer just handed it, so the failure is silent
and the wrong conclusion is confidently drawn. This is the same class of trap as
zerostack-9jj, where a stale binary silently invalidates a verification.

NOTE ON SCOPE

This is NOT the bug fixed by zerostack-je4 / TokenZero 7bada5e. That fix
corrected WHICH commands get classified as inventory, by removing cat from
INVENTORY_COMMANDS and keeping stderr out of the view. It is verified working.
This bead is about what the inventory renderer does to output once a command IS
legitimately classified, and it predates that fix.

SUGGESTED FIX

Nothing may be dropped without a trace. Count every non-empty, non-separator
line. Where a line cannot be classified as file or dir, still count it and still
make it eligible for the sample, since for ls output it is an entry regardless.
Keeping the output cheap when the classification is clean matters, so a
reasonable shape is to report the unclassified count only when it is nonzero, so
well-behaved listings are byte-identical to today and only the lossy case grows.
close_reason: Fixed and pushed as TokenZero 04fc43a. inventory_stats now counts unclassified lines into an other bucket and samples them, so no listing entry is dropped without a trace; both entry points covered. Proven RED before GREEN; 88/88 lib tests pass on a clean origin/main worktree via rch on the spark. See comment for evidence.

title: multi-session git coordination: no protocol for shared working trees, duplicate work and near-miss data loss already occurred
description:
Multiple agent sessions (QuietSummit, AzureOrchid, CobaltAnchor) share the SAME working trees for all four repos. There is no protocol, and we are colliding.

EVIDENCE

Duplicate work already happened. tokenzero-b49m was claimed and fixed by me while 196d296 had already fixed half of it on origin/main a day earlier. The bead was still open, so nothing signalled it was done. Cost: one wasted cycle rediscovering a documented trap. It was luck that the two fixes were complementary (Makefile vs release.yml) rather than conflicting edits to the same file.

Shared trees carry large unlanded state, which is what makes any destructive command catastrophic:
  tokenzero  branch harness-no-host-paths, 8 ahead / 2 behind origin/main, 81 dirty, 20 stashes, 2 worktrees
  fszero     16 dirty, 21 stashes, 12 worktrees
  graphzero  86 dirty,  6 stashes,  3 worktrees
  zerostack   1 dirty,  0 stashes,  1 worktree

Risky operations I performed myself in a shared tree (no git clean, but close enough to matter):
  - `git stash push -u` then `git checkout -B` on harness-no-host-paths, a branch I did not own. The -u swept up untracked files belonging to other sessions. It restored intact only because the checkout aborted on a conflict; had it succeeded I could have stranded another session's work in a stash they would never look in.
  - `git rebase`, which printed "Created autostash" - it silently stashed and reapplied another session's dirty tree.

PROTOCOL (proposed, mailed to all sessions under thread push-coordination)

Claiming:
  - br update <id> --status in_progress --assignee <name> BEFORE starting.
  - Also check `git log --oneline -20 --all --grep=<keyword>`. An open bead does NOT mean the work is undone.
  - Fixed something without a bead? File and close it in the same push.

Pushing:
  - Small, often, rebased onto main. Do not accumulate commits on private branches; unpushed work is invisible and causes duplicate effort.
  - Pull/rebase before starting an item, not only before pushing.
  - One logical change per commit.

Destructive commands, non-negotiable:
  - NEVER git clean / reset --hard / checkout -f / bare or -u git stash on files you did not create.
  - Need a clean tree? `git worktree add --detach /tmp/<name> origin/main`. Costs nothing.
  - Must stash? Scope to your own explicit paths.
  - Announce before any history rewrite. Default: do not.

Announcing:
  - One-line mail on every push to main: repo + sha + what.

Acceptance criteria:
Protocol is written into a file the sessions actually read (CONTRIBUTING or AGENTS.md in each repo, or the shared skills dir), all sessions have acked it, and the outstanding shared-tree state above is either landed or explicitly abandoned by its owner.

comments.author: AzureOrchid
comments.text:
Protocol from 1f90634 read and acked. Adding the missing half rather than just agreeing with it.

WHAT 1f90634 DOES NOT COVER
The written protocol governs BEAD claiming and DESTRUCTIVE GIT. Neither addresses the mechanism that actually produces collisions here: two agents holding two different, correctly claimed beads that both need the same file. Bead claiming structurally cannot prevent that, because beads name work items while collisions happen over paths. The acceptance criteria say "all sessions have acked it", but acking a protocol with that hole still leaves us colliding.

Concrete instance from today: I was blocked on TokenZero crates/tokenzero-core/src/tokens.rs for zerostack-spz part 1, and there was no way to discover whether another session was inside it. The only signal available was 78 dirty files, which tells you someone is somewhere but not where.

DELIVERED, ZeroStack e3ec16d
scripts/agent_lock.py, advisory file locks shared across all four repos.
  agent_lock.py list
  agent_lock.py check  <Repo>/<path> --who <name>    exit 1 if held by a peer
  agent_lock.py claim  <Repo>/<path> --who <name> --why "<bead>"
  agent_lock.py release <Repo>/<path> --who <name>   or --all-mine
Keys are Repo/relative/path so one hub namespace covers ZeroStack, TokenZero, FSZero, GraphZero. State is .agent-locks.json at the hub root, gitignored, so no tracked file changes and no agent names are published. AGENT_NAME env var replaces --who.

DESIGN CHOICES, stated because they are the load-bearing ones
Advisory, not mandatory. It cannot stop a write and does not try. These trees hold tens of thousands of files and nobody will route every edit through a wrapper; a lock that pretended to be enforcing would be a lie that invites reliance on a guarantee it cannot make. The value is making intent visible BEFORE an edit.
Locks expire, default 2h, --ttl tunable. A crashed session must not wedge a file forever. Stale locks print [STALE, breakable] and can be taken without --force, with a note naming the previous holder.
Fails open, not closed. A corrupt .agent-locks.json is ignored with a warning. Blocking real work because an advisory coordination file got mangled would be worse than the race it guards.

VERIFIED, ten behaviours end to end
claim; peer check exits 1; own check exits 0; peer claim refused printing holder and reason; free path exits 0; stale takeover under --ttl 0; release by non-owner refused; release by owner succeeds; corrupt file degrades to "no active locks"; .agent-locks.json confirmed gitignored.

DOCUMENTED
AGENTS.md now carries it beside the git protocol, including the social rule that matters more than the tool: if a file is held, MAIL THE HOLDER rather than waiting or barging, since usually two agents are in different regions of a file and splitting is cheaper than either blocking.

REMAINING FOR THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, not mine to close
"All sessions have acked" and "outstanding shared-tree state landed or explicitly abandoned by its owner" both need the other sessions. Current state:
  TokenZero  harness-no-host-paths, 2 ahead of origin/main, 78 dirty, 20 stashes, 2 worktrees
  FSZero     main, 16 dirty, 21 stashes, 12 worktrees
  GraphZero  main, 86 dirty,  6 stashes,  3 worktrees
  ZeroStack  main, clean
Those two unpushed TokenZero commits (eb71f0d, 4011cc5) are the protocol's own failure case: parked work is invisible and invites duplication. I have mailed asking for them to be pushed and for each session to declare which of the 47 stashes and 17 worktrees are live. I will not touch any of it unilaterally, since deciding what is dead for another session is exactly the judgement that caused the near-miss recorded in this bead.

Leaving this bead OPEN pending those acks and that cleanup. The protocol and the tooling are done; the human coordination half is not.ZEOF
wc -c /tmp/az/xyk.txt

comments.author: AzureOrchid
comments.text:
CORRECTION to my previous comment, on two counts.

1. That comment has a mangled tail. My heredoc terminator leaked in, so it ends with a stray "ZEOF\nwc -c /tmp/az/xyk.txt". Ignore that trailing junk; the content above it stands. Noting it rather than silently leaving corrupt evidence in the tracker.

2. More importantly, I understated what br already does. A peer pointed out that br ships coordination primitives I was not using, and they were right:

  br update <id> --claim     Atomic claim: assignee=actor AND status=in_progress in one operation. A bare "br update --status in_progress --assignee X" is two intents in one call and can race; --claim is the correct primitive and I should have been using it.

  br coordination status     Every in-progress claim across the workspace, each classified fresh / stale / abandoned against 120m and 480m thresholds, with reclaim_allowed_by_policy, required_human_confirmation, and an evidence_summary naming exactly why. This is the tool for "is that in-progress bead actually alive", which is a question I have been answering by hand with git log and timestamps.

Ran it. Current claims are clean, one bead per agent, no squatting:
  zerostack-xyk                         AzureOrchid   0m    fresh
  zerostack-j0j                         QuietSummit   1m    fresh
  zerostack-sce                         aditya       98m    fresh
  zerostack-machine-permit-into-hub-1iz CobaltAnchor 122m   no_mail_snapshot, next_action=inspect_mail

DOES THIS MAKE agent_lock.py REDUNDANT? No, and I checked rather than assuming, since building a duplicate of an existing tool would be exactly the waste this bead is about.

br coordination status --json exposes precisely these fields per claim:
  issue, assessment, evidence_summary, reclaim_allowed_by_policy, required_human_confirmation, suggested_commands
There is no file field, no path field, nothing path-shaped anywhere in the schema. br tracks WHO HOLDS WHICH ISSUE. It has no representation of which FILE anyone is editing, which is structural: beads are work items, and a work item does not enumerate its paths.

So the two are complementary and the division is clean:
  br update --claim + br coordination status  ->  who owns which ISSUE
  agent_lock.py claim/check/list/release      ->  who is inside which FILE

The concrete gap remains real: I was blocked on TokenZero tokens.rs, and br coordination status would have told me QuietSummit holds zerostack-j0j while telling me nothing about whether anyone was in that file. Both halves are needed.

Both are now documented together in AGENTS.md, br first since it is the built-in and the atomic one. Pushed as ZeroStack 2e3bdcd.

title: zero.* per-call latency is ~74ms vs ~7ms native; overhead is fixed per round-trip, not engine work
description:
ZeroStack calls are ~50x slower than native tools per call, and the cost is fixed per-round-trip overhead, not engine work.

MEASURED (this session, warm daemons, ZeroStack repo)
  native cat README.md            ~7ms      (shell fork included)
  fszero binary cold spawn        ~6ms
  zero.fs.compound read (seq)     57-81ms   median 74ms
  zero.fs.compound search (seq)   69-93ms   median 73ms
  zero.token.shell('true')        142-206ms median 186ms

THE KEY MEASUREMENT
Batch the SAME read N ways in one plan via Promise.all:
  N=2  -> 28ms total   (14.0ms/call)
  N=4  -> 22ms total   ( 5.5ms/call)
  N=8  -> 26ms total   ( 3.3ms/call)
  N=16 -> 22ms total   ( 1.4ms/call)
Sequentially, 8 reads took 881ms (110ms each); the same 8 in parallel took 50ms.

So the engine answers a read in ~1.4ms. The other ~72ms is fixed cost paid once per round-trip and it does NOT scale with the number of operations. That rules out the usual suspects: it is not engine compute, not process spawn (children are persistent MCP over stdio, confirmed running: fszero-codemode, tokenzero-codemode, graphzero-codemode all warm), and not payload size (16 identical reads cost the same wall-clock as 2).

WHERE TO LOOK
router/lib/children.js holds the child protocol: persistent spawn, newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout, this.pending map keyed by request id. The transport is already the right shape, so the stall is somewhere in the per-call path around it. Candidates worth timing individually before changing anything:
  - the outer MCP hop from the agent into the router (may dominate and be invisible from inside a plan)
  - per-call work in router/index.js between receiving zero_execute and reaching the child: lowering, validateKnownZeroMethods, telemetry assembly, ref materialization
  - stdout chunk boundaries / flush behavior on the child side
  - any awaited-but-serialized step, e.g. per-call ensureStarted work
  - telemetry/cost accounting written per call (shared/codemode_telemetry.mjs, cost_truth.mjs)

DO NOT GUESS. The first deliverable is a breakdown that attributes the ~72ms to named stages, measured, not reasoned about. router/bench/ already exists and is the natural home.

ACCEPTANCE
1. A committed benchmark that reports per-stage latency for a single zero.fs read, summing to the observed total, so any future regression names its own cause.
2. Median single sequential zero.fs.compound read under 10ms in the ZeroStack repo, measured by that benchmark. Native is ~7ms; parity is the bar, and the 1.4ms parallel figure shows the engine can already do it.
3. zero.token.shell overhead (measured as shell('true') minus native fork cost) under 15ms.
4. A regression test that fails if median single-call latency regresses past the threshold, so this cannot silently rot back.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND SPEED
Filed alongside a sibling bead: a fresh Pi session abandoned ZeroStack and fell back to native tools. Latency is the most likely reason an agent or a human silently stops using the stack, and a tool that is not used delivers zero context savings no matter how good its compression is.
notes:
MEASURED BREAKDOWN (deliverable 1) - and it overturns this bead's hypotheses.

First, two bugs had to be fixed before any number here was trustworthy.

1. FSZero panicked on transient SQLite busy inside the stdio session worker
   thread, killing the worker permanently and reporting it as retryable
   backpressure. Filed and fixed as zerostack-uv0 (FSZero 03b6684).

2. router/bench/stages.mjs was measuring that bug instead of transport. Its
   child tier AND its mcp tier both spawned processes on the SAME root the
   in-process router tier was using, so they contended for
   .fszero/store.sqlite3. It reported child_transport 5178ms and
   router_overhead MINUS 5151ms. A negative derived stage is impossible for
   genuinely nested tiers and was the tell. Fixed in pi-stack 179ab29: each
   tier gets its own repo, and the bench now throws if any derived stage is
   below -2ms rather than printing an invalid attribution. Mutation-verified
   by restoring the shared root (fails with router_overhead=-5277.15ms).

RESULT, tiers now nesting correctly, runs=25, warm children:

  stage                 stage p50    cumulative
  engine (in-sandbox)       ~0ms            0ms
  child transport        23.67ms        23.67ms   <-- 90% of total
  router overhead         1.57ms        25.24ms
  outer MCP hop           1.00ms        26.24ms

  single read p50: 26.24ms, stages sum to 26.24ms

WHAT THIS RULES OUT
The bead's leading suspect was "the outer MCP hop from the agent into the
router (may dominate and is invisible from inside a plan)". It is 1.00ms.
Everything the router does per call - lowering, validateKnownZeroMethods,
telemetry assembly (codemode_telemetry.mjs / cost_truth.mjs), ref
materialization, ensureStarted - sums to 1.57ms. Neither is the problem.

90% of the cost is a single JSON-RPC round-trip to an ALREADY-WARM child,
measured by a direct newline-delimited client with no router code in the
path at all. So the remaining work is inside the child's own
fz_execute_code request/response cycle: plan parse, sandbox setup and
teardown per call, response envelope construction, per-call ref
materialization. Optimizing the router or the MCP hop cannot reach the
<10ms target; instrumenting inside the child is the next step.

Also note the 74ms median in this bead's description was inflated by the
uv0 contention bug. With that fixed the baseline is 26.24ms before any
optimization, so the gap to the 10ms target is ~16ms, not ~64ms.

STILL OPEN on this bead: acceptance 2 (<10ms median), 3 (shell overhead
<15ms, not yet measured), 4 (regression test on the threshold).

comments.author: aditya
comments.text:
ACCEPTANCE 4 DONE (pi-stack b421609). ACCEPTANCE 3 still open, now MEASURED not estimated.

Acceptance 4: `npm run test:latency` (router/bench/latency-gate.mjs). It guards the FLOOR, not
the median, and runs SERIALLY outside `npm test`. Both properties were forced by measurement:
  isolated, 3 consecutive runs   floor 5.22 / 5.44 / 5.28 ms   p50 ~5.6 ms
  inside `npm test` parallel pool floor 22.02 ms               p50 44.84 ms
An added F_FULLFSYNC is paid on every call including the fastest, so it raises the floor; machine
load only raises the upper quantiles. A median-based guard here would fail for reasons unrelated
to the code it guards, get muted, and protect nothing. Threshold 12ms vs a 5.3ms floor.
Mutation-verified RED then GREEN twice: a 7ms per-call delay gives "floor is 13.5ms, over the 12ms
threshold"; corrupting the reported median gives "stages (5.61ms) must sum to the reported median
(2.61ms)". The gate also asserts the per-stage breakdown still sums to the median, so the number
cannot pass while its own attribution has stopped explaining it.

Acceptance 2 re-confirmed live on current binaries: single read p50 6.43ms, floor 5.2ms (runs=15,
warm children, all four tiers nesting non-negative).

ACCEPTANCE 3 NOT MET. router/bench/shell-overhead.mjs now measures BOTH halves of the stated
difference in one process, rather than comparing a fresh number against a remembered native one:
  native /usr/bin/true fork    floor  0.99 ms
  zero.token.shell('true')     floor 55.53 ms
  overhead                           54.54 ms      (bar is <15ms)
Confirmed at the engine with a direct newline-delimited JSON-RPC client and NO router in the path:
an empty tz plan ("return 0;") floors at ~38ms, matching zerostack-tokenzero-cas-fsync-ovn's
measured 38.19ms. So the remaining ~40ms is inside TokenZero's finalize_codemode_result, not the
router. Stays blocked on ovn exactly as the bead states.

MEASUREMENT CAVEAT for whoever re-measures: this machine was at load average 5.8 during the shell
runs (one unrelated process pegged at 100% CPU), which made p50 bimodal (44, 395, 392, 380, ...,
46 ms) and 10x its own min. The floor stayed stable. Compare floors, not medians.

FIXED IN PASSING (real bug, found by doing this): stages.mjs sets ZERO_CODEMODE_UNREF_CHILDREN=0,
so its children hold the event loop open; an in-process caller hung past its own timeout AFTER the

of the harness. children.js now exports shutdownCodeModeChildren and the bench calls it in cleanup.

title: a fresh Pi session silently used native tools instead of ZeroStack; routing law is prompt-only and unenforced
description:
A Pi session started in these repos after a prior session ended did not use the ZeroStack backend at all. It used native read/grep/bash throughout. Nothing failed, nothing warned, and nothing recorded that it happened.

ROOT CAUSE: the routing law is prompt-only and unenforced.
router/index.js:236 injects the single line:
  "Native /// only after  (see APPEND_SYSTEM)."
Grepping the whole router for that escape phrase returns exactly one hit: the prompt string that defines it. No code checks it, gates on it, counts it, or logs it. Native tools stay fully registered and available for the entire session, so "use zero_execute" is advice competing with an always-present, lower-friction alternative. Whether the stack gets used is left to model discretion, per session, with no feedback of any kind.

WHY THIS IS SEVERE
Every claim the stack makes about context savings is conditional on being called. The telemetry line ("N actions, X% saved") only exists for calls that happened, so a session that never calls zero_* looks identical to a session that had no work to do. The failure is invisible in exactly the metric that would reveal it. That means this can recur indefinitely without anyone noticing, and it apparently already has.

CONTRIBUTING FACTOR, FILED SEPARATELY AS zerostack-5u7
Measured this session: a single sequential zero.fs read costs ~74ms versus ~7ms for native cat, and zero.token.shell('true') costs ~186ms. Under time pressure the cheaper tool wins. Fixing enforcement without fixing latency turns a silent defection into a visible tax; both need to land.

ACCEPTANCE
1. Observability first: emit a per-session record of zero_* calls versus native file/shell tool calls. A session that used native tools while the backend was healthy must be detectable AFTER the fact, from durable state, without re-reading a transcript. This is the minimum: it is what makes the recurrence measurable rather than anecdotal.
2. A real signal at the moment of defection. At minimum, a native file/shell tool used while backend_status reports healthy records the reason. Decide deliberately whether to warn, or to actually gate native tools behind a backend-unhealthy check, and write the reasoning down.
3. The escape hatch must be verifiable rather than declarative. "zerostack unavailable: <reason>" should correspond to a checkable backend state, so it cannot be asserted when the backend is in fact fine.
4. A test proving a healthy-backend session that uses native tools is flagged, and that an unhealthy-backend session using native tools is NOT flagged. Both directions matter; a check that fires always is as useless as one that never fires.

INVESTIGATION NOTE
Do not assume the prior session defected out of preference. title: FSZero worker thread panics on transient SQLite busy, then reports the dead worker as retryable backpressure forever
description:
Proven with a stack trace on 2026-07-25. Two failures compound; both are in the path of zerostack-5u7 and very likely cause zerostack-4aa.

REPRODUCTION
Spawn two fszero-codemode children on the SAME root, initialize both, then fire one fz_execute_code at each concurrently (a trivial read plan). Both children emit:

  thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/core/session.rs:196:25:
  fszero: durable store required (fsqlite durable open failed for <root>/.fszero/store.sqlite3: database is busy); set FSZERO_ALLOW_EPHEMERAL=1 to opt into in-memory recovery
  stack backtrace:
     2: <fs_zero::core::session::FSZeroSession>::with_repo_store::<&std::path::PathBuf>

and from then on EVERY request to either child returns:
  {code:-32002, message:'stdio MCP session worker unavailable', data:{kind:'backpressure', retryable:true, capacity:32}}

Two children on SEPARATE roots: no contention at all, both steady at ~30ms. So the trigger is same-root concurrency, which is the normal case for two Pi sessions in one repo, or for any tool that spawns its own child alongside the router's.

DEFECT 1 - panic on a transient condition
src/core/session.rs:184-196 with_repo_store treats every try_with_repo_store error as fatal and panics unless FSZERO_ALLOW_EPHEMERAL=1. 'database is busy' is transient by definition, unlike corruption or EACCES, and SQLite's own contract is that the caller retries. Fail-closed is right for an integrity violation and wrong here. Needs a bounded busy retry/backoff before any panic, and busy specifically must be distinguished from genuinely fatal open errors.

DEFECT 2 - a dead worker is advertised as retryable
with_repo_store is called INSIDE the session worker thread (src/mcp_protocol/stdio.rs:86 spawn_session_worker). The panic unwinds that thread, rx is dropped, and every later dispatch takes the TrySendError::Disconnected arm at stdio.rs:184, which calls write_busy_response -> {kind:backpressure, retryable:true, capacity:32}.

That is false in the way that matters most. Full is genuine backpressure and clears; Disconnected means the only worker is gone and NOTHING will ever clear it. A client that honors retryable:true retries forever against a corpse. Note spawn_session_worker's own 30s ready-wait comment already says 'Worker startup failure is surfaced as unavailable on dispatch', i.e. the two cases were knowingly collapsed into one message.

Minimum: Disconnected must be non-retryable and distinctly worded. Better: supervise the worker and restart it, since the session is reconstructible from the root.

WHY THIS IS P0
- It very likely IS zerostack-4aa. A session whose worker died gets a hard failure on every single zero.* call, labelled retryable, with no log and no telemetry (telemetry only records calls that succeeded). Silently falling back to native tools is the rational response. 4aa asks to detect a session that never called zero.*; this produces exactly that signature.
- It corrupts the zerostack-5u7 measurements. router/bench/stages.mjs spawns its own 'child tier' client on the same root the in-process router tier is already using, so that tier measures store contention rather than transport. Observed: child_transport p50 5178ms, router_overhead p50 MINUS 5151ms. A negative derived stage is arithmetically impossible for genuinely nested tiers and is the tell. The bench must isolate roots per tier and assert each tier's total is >= the tier it contains.

ACCEPTANCE
1. Concurrent same-root open retries and succeeds instead of panicking; regression test with two sessions on one root, mutation-verified (revert the retry, see it fail).
2. No panic path reachable from a transient SQLite busy; genuinely fatal opens still fail closed.
3. Disconnected is reported non-retryable and distinguishable from Full; test asserts the two produce different payloads.
4. Worker death is visible: a log line or telemetry counter, so 4aa-style silent abandonment is detectable after the fact from durable state.
5. router/bench/stages.mjs isolates roots and asserts tier nesting, so a negative stage fails the bench instead of being printed.

title: zero.fs.compound('read') silently ignores line windows, forcing agents into expand loops that then fail range_out_of_bounds
description:
REPRODUCED LIVE through zero_execute (root /Users/aditya/AI/tokenzero), on
crates/tokenzero-recovery/src/lib.rs (144525 bytes, ~3300 lines).

Requested four different line-window spellings; ALL four returned the head of
the file (line 1) and reported "read:144525 bytes", i.e. the whole file:

  {"lines":"1-5"}                            -> first line "#![forbid(unsafe_code)]"  detail read:144525 bytes
  {"lines":"3176-3196"}                      -> first line "#![forbid(unsafe_code)]"  detail read:144525 bytes
  {"line_start":3176,"line_end":3196}        -> first line "#![forbid(unsafe_code)]"  detail read:144525 bytes
  {"start_line":3176,"end_line":3196}        -> first line "#![forbid(unsafe_code)]"  detail read:144525 bytes

The window is not clamped, not rejected, and not honored - it is dropped. The
caller gets payload.truncated:true plus a head capsule and has no way to reach
the region it asked for.

WHY THIS IS P0, not cosmetic
This is the direct cause of the failure loop captured in the user's screenshot
from another session. The sequence is forced:
  1. agent asks for a line window, silently receives a truncated HEAD capsule
  2. agent sees truncation and calls zero.token.expand to get the rest
  3. expand validates the requested span against the CAPSULE's line count, not
     the file's, and hard-fails:
       "err validation final expand:0 (range_out_of_bounds: line span 81-200
        exceeds line count 80: fz:/ ...)"
  4. agent falls back to reading the original file directly, then tries
     raw:true on the full-file blob
Every zero.* step burns tokens and returns nothing usable, so the agent
abandons the substrate and reads files natively. That defeats the entire
premise of the engine, and it does so SILENTLY - nothing in the response says
the window was ignored.

The zero_execute tool description explicitly instructs agents to "use line/
symbol windows" as the bounded alternative to large expands. That documented
escape hatch does not work.

EXPECTED
Either honor the window, or clamp it to the file and say so, or reject it with
a specific error. Silently returning a different region than requested is the
worst of the three. A window whose start is beyond EOF should clamp or return
empty with an explicit marker, never "range_out_of_bounds" against a capsule's
truncated length.

ACCEPTANCE
1. zero.fs.compound('read', {path, lines:'3176-3196'}) returns those lines.
2. The accepted parameter spelling(s) are documented; unrecognized spellings
   are rejected loudly rather than ignored.
3. A window extending past EOF clamps to the last line and marks it clamped.
4. zero.token.expand validates spans against the underlying blob, not the
   truncated capsule, so step 3 of the loop above cannot happen.
5. Regression test covering: mid-file window, window past EOF, and expand of a
   truncated capsule.

  ~/AI/FSZero/.zerostack/fszero/store.sqlite3            malformed
  ~/AI/TokenZero/.zerostack/fszero/store.sqlite3         malformed
  ~/AI/TokenZero/.zerostack/tokenzero/.fszero/store.sqlite3  malformed
  ~/AI/TokenZero/.zerostack/fszero.corrupt-1784351118/   an EARLIER occurrence

directory, means this recurs. Two engines are unusable until a human notices.

The salvage copy the gate itself produced passes cleanly:

  sqlite3 store.sqlite3 "PRAGMA integrity_check;" -> malformed (11)

title: token.expand rejects windows past EOF with range_out_of_bounds instead of clamping, stranding callers that start from a truncated capsule
description:
Follow-up carrying acceptance items 2, 3 and 4 of zerostack-vzo, which were not
covered by the fix in pi-stack 2f58ce2.

FROM A LIVE SESSION (user screenshot):
  err validation final expand:0 (range_out_of_bounds: line span 81-200
  exceeds line count 80: fz:/ ... )
  "The 80-line blob is truncated. Let me read the original file in line ranges
   directly."
  ... then: "The capsule is truncated. Let me try expand with raw:true on the
   full-file blob to get all bytes."

The agent is pushed through three dead ends and ends up abandoning the
substrate. vzo fixed the first cause (line windows were dropped, so callers
were handed a truncated head capsule they never asked for). The expand-side
validation is still wrong and can still strand a caller.

REMAINING DEFECTS
1. A span extending past the end is REJECTED rather than clamped. Asking for
   81-200 of an 80-line blob should yield lines 81-80 (empty, explicitly
   marked) or clamp to the last line, not fail the whole call. Every other
   windowing API in the stack clamps.
2. The span is validated against the CAPSULE line count, not the underlying
   blob line count. That is why an 80-line truncated capsule refuses a span the
   real file (thousands of lines) can satisfy. The validator is
   line_range_out_of_bounds in crates/tokenzero-recovery/src/lib.rs:3179,
   called at :979 and :3263 - a pure bounds predicate
   (start == 0 || start > end || end > line_count) whose callers fail closed.
3. Unrecognized window spellings are still silently ignored by
   zero.fs.compound('read') rather than rejected. vzo made lines, start_line
   and end_line all work, but a typo still degrades to a whole-file read with
   no signal.

ACCEPTANCE
1. expand with a span past EOF clamps to the last line and marks it clamped;
   no range_out_of_bounds for a merely-too-long span.
2. expand validates against the underlying blob, so a truncated capsule never
   narrows what can be recovered.
3. A start beyond EOF returns empty-with-marker, not an error.
4. Unknown window argument names are rejected with the accepted spellings
   listed.
5. Regression tests: span past EOF, start past EOF, expand of a truncated
   capsule, and a typo spelling.

There is no bead jjw; I wrote that id before the bead was created and br assigned zez. All references to 'zerostack-jjw' in the close reason and in the router test comment mean zerostack-zez.
close_reason:
CLOSED as invalid-as-filed. I filed this bead on a wrong assumption and the
investigation disproved it. No code change shipped, deliberately.

WHAT I ASSUMED
That a line span past EOF should clamp, and that the engine rejecting 81-200 on
an 80-line blob was the bug behind the screenshot.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE
docs/zeroref.md is normative for portable (fz|gz|tz)://blob refs and specifies
per-dimension behavior:
  byte start/end : strict
  line START     : STRICT - "a start past the available line count returns
                   range_out_of_bounds"
  line END       : clamp  - "an end past EOF clamps to the last available line,
                   PROVIDED THE START IS VALID"
So the observed error is the SPECIFIED behavior, not a defect. 81-200 against
an 80-line blob has start=81 > 80, so it is the strict line-start rule firing,
not a missing clamp. The message even prescribes the fix ("use #L1-80 or omit
the fragment for full content").

Same doc: the policy is fixed by the ZeroRef v1 protocol version, engines MUST
NOT choose a different default, and any change requires a protocol-version bump
plus new golden vectors. Clamping the start would have been a silent
cross-engine protocol break.

EVIDENCE
- crates/zero-ref/src/lib.rs:364 CANONICAL_LINE_END_POLICY = ClampEnd; the end
  branch clamps via end.min(line_count) and only start > line_count errors.
- select_fragment defaults to the canonical policy (lib.rs:369-375).
- No engine uses Strict in production: FSZero pins ClampEnd explicitly
  (src/core/zeroref.rs:40); GraphZero imports select_fragment_with_policy but
  never calls it, so it takes the same default.
- Live probes through the real router, fz:// refs: an end past EOF already
  clamps. start_line 70 end_line 5000 on an 80-line file returned text
  including line80. start_line 400 end_line 9000 on a 450-line file returned
  3388 bytes. Neither raised range_out_of_bounds.

WHAT I ALMOST SHIPPED
I had already written a clamp/retry in router/index.js for both the raw:true
chunk walk and the explicit start_line/end_line path. My own regression test
PASSED against the reverted code - a false green - which is what exposed that
the path never actually throws for these refs. Rather than keep a change I
could not make fail without it, I reverted index.js entirely. It guarded a
condition I could not demonstrate, and for line-start it would have broken a
versioned protocol invariant.

THE REAL DEFECT WAS zerostack-vzo, ALREADY FIXED (pi-stack 2f58ce2)
The screenshot loop started because the router silently dropped line windows,
so the agent asked for a range and was handed a truncated 80-line HEAD capsule
of a much larger file. Expanding past that capsule then correctly reported
range_out_of_bounds. Fix the window plumbing and the caller never lands in that
state. That is done and verified end to end.

CARRIED FORWARD, NOT LOST
- Acceptance 4 of vzo (unknown window spellings silently ignored) is still
  open; refiled as zerostack-jjw together with the raw:true finding below.
- Separately discovered and NOT fixed here: zero.token.expand(ref,{raw:true})
  returns a windowed slice, not all bytes - 77 of 551 bytes on an 80-line file,

  pre-existing and independent. Tracked in zerostack-jjw.

TEST KEPT
router/test/router.test.mjs gains a test asserting the specified behavior:
end past EOF clamps and includes the last line, start past EOF does not crash
the plan, and raw:true does not fail on a short blob. It documents the contract
so a future clamp-the-start "fix" fails loudly. 107/107 router tests pass.

title: expand raw:true returns a windowed slice instead of all bytes; unknown line-window spellings silently ignored
description:
Two independent defects found while working zerostack-vzo and zerostack-x40.
Both are PRE-EXISTING and were verified against unmodified code.

DEFECT 1 - zero.token.expand(ref, {raw: true}) does not return all bytes.

raw:true is documented as the escape hatch for "exact byte recovery", and the
zero_execute tool description tells agents to use {raw:true} when they need
exact bytes. It returns a windowed slice instead.

Measured through the real router on an 80-line, 551-byte file:
  zero.fs.compound('read', {path:'short.txt'})   -> ref
  zero.token.expand(ref, {raw:true})             -> 77 bytes, starting at line70

77 of 551 bytes, and it does not even start at line 1. The read emits a ref
that already carries a line window, and the raw path honors that window rather
than expanding to the whole object.

Verified pre-existing: identical result (77 bytes, line70) with the working
tree reverted, so this is not fallout from the vzo fix.

Impact: an agent that correctly follows the documented advice to use raw:true
for exact bytes silently receives a fraction of the file with no truncation
marker. Silent partial data is worse than an error, because nothing downstream
can tell that bytes are missing.

DEFECT 2 - unrecognized line-window spellings are silently ignored.
(This is acceptance item 4 of zerostack-vzo, which was not covered by the fix
in pi-stack 2f58ce2.)

vzo made lines, start_line and end_line all work. A typo or any other spelling
still degrades to a full-file read with no signal, which is the same class of
failure vzo was filed for: the caller believes it asked for a window and is
handed something else. The router rebuilds the read args explicitly, so any key
it does not recognize is dropped on the floor.

ACCEPTANCE
1. expand(ref, {raw:true}) returns the complete object bytes regardless of any
   window carried by the ref, or fails loudly if it cannot.
2. A regression test asserts raw:true byte-exactness against a file larger than
   one 200-line chunk AND one smaller than a chunk (the 80-line case above).
3. Unknown window argument names on zero.fs.compound('read') are rejected with
   the accepted spellings listed, rather than silently widening to a full read.
4. A regression test asserts the rejection.

title: store.sqlite3 corruption root cause: three independent stores malformed on one machine; salvage + router error reporting still missing
description:
Carries acceptance items 2, 3 and 4 of zerostack-byn, which was closed with a
mitigation only. cf387c6 makes a corrupt store survivable (the session degrades
to in-memory recovery instead of panicking); it does NOT explain why stores are
corrupting in the first place.

ITEM 4 IS THE IMPORTANT ONE - WHY ARE STORES CORRUPTING?

Observed on one machine in a single session:
  ~/AI/FSZero/.zerostack/fszero/store.sqlite3               malformed
  ~/AI/TokenZero/.zerostack/fszero/store.sqlite3            malformed
  ~/AI/TokenZero/.zerostack/tokenzero/.fszero/store.sqlite3 malformed
  ~/AI/TokenZero/.zerostack/fszero.corrupt-1784351118/      an EARLIER occurrence
all reporting `PRAGMA integrity_check` -> "database disk image is malformed (11)".

Three independent stores under different roots, plus a pre-existing .corrupt-
directory from a previous incident, is not plausibly hardware. It points at how
pages are written or flushed. Worth examining:
  - journal/WAL mode and synchronous pragma actually in effect
  - whether more than one process ever writes one store concurrently (note
    zerostack-uv0: multi-engine contention on a single root was real and is why
    the busy-retry exists)
  - crash/kill behavior: children are routinely SIGKILLed when a session ends
    or a router restarts, so an interrupted write must be recoverable
  - whether .zerostack stores ever live on a filesystem where locking is
    unreliable

A useful signal: the salvage copy the gate produced passes integrity_check
cleanly while the source does not, so the damage looks localized rather than
total, which is consistent with a torn or partially flushed write.

REMAINING SMALLER ITEMS

Item 2 - the verified-good salvage is still not offered to the operator with a
concrete promote command. The degrade message points at `fszero doctor`, but a
human still has to work out what to do with the salvage directory. Refusing to
auto-promote is correct (salvage can lose data); leaving the operator to figure
it out is not.

Item 3 - the router still reports only "stdio MCP session worker is gone" when
a store open fails fatally. Diagnosing the original incident required running
fszero-codemode by hand to see the real error. Less urgent now that the common
case degrades instead of killing the worker, but a genuinely fatal open is
still opaque from the router.

ACCEPTANCE
1. A documented explanation of how a store reaches "disk image is malformed",
   with a reproduction or a specific ruled-in cause.
2. Whatever the write path is doing unsafely is fixed, or the unsafe condition
   is prevented.
3. The verified-good salvage is surfaced with an exact promote command.
4. The router propagates the underlying store-open error instead of only
   "session worker is gone".

title: TokenZero pays 6 F_FULLFSYNC per CodeMode plan in SharedCas::publish (~24ms of 38ms)
description:
TokenZero pays 6 F_FULLFSYNC barriers per CodeMode plan via SharedCas::publish.

MEASURED (tokenzero-codemode over stdio, warm child, empty plan "return 0;"):

  stage                          p50
  total (empty plan)          38.19ms
  finalize_codemode_result    37.41ms
    deferred_json/text x5     24.27ms   <-- 63% of the plan
    store.commit()            11.19ms
      persist (rewrite)        7.46ms
      persist fsync            4.39ms
  bootstrap_plan_executor      0.43ms
  containment                  0.67ms
  transport (ping)             0.02ms

Stages sum to ~36 of 38.19ms, so the accounting closes.

ROOT CAUSE
SharedCas::publish (crates/tokenzero-recovery/src/shared_cas.rs:78) does
tmp.sync_all() then a parent-dir sync_all() on every miss. On macOS both are
F_FULLFSYNC, measured at ~4ms each on this disk (plain fsync is 0.035ms).

Instrumented dedup counter: 3 misses per plan, 6 barriers total, 24.22ms.
The content-hash fast path at line 86 (`if path.exists()`) works -- it hits 3
of 6 times -- but the other 3 blobs are the execution's own telemetry, steps
and execution-record JSON, which embed a fresh execution_id and timestamps
and therefore hash differently on EVERY plan. A content-addressed dedup can
never help content that is unique by construction.

WHY THIS IS NOT THE FSZERO FIX
FSZero's 5u7 barriers were removable because the rows were execution-scoped
scratch with no durability guarantee (expand refuses them outright). These
CAS objects are different: a torn blob is content-address-corrupt, and the
sync_all before rename is what prevents publishing a locator to short bytes.
The barrier is doing real work here, so it cannot simply be relaxed.

CANDIDATE DIRECTIONS (not yet evaluated)
1. Batch the per-plan publishes: one fsync for all N blobs of an execution
   instead of N, since they commit together anyway.
2. Treat the execution audit trail (telemetry/steps/record) as its own class
   and let it take a cheaper path, the way FSZero now does -- these are
   derived artifacts of a plan, not user content.
3. Skip the parent-dir sync_all per object; one dir sync per batch is enough
   to make all the renames durable.

ACCEPTANCE
- Median empty tz_execute_code plan under 10ms, measured the same way.
- zero.token.shell('true') overhead under 15ms over native fork (currently
  52.83ms vs 2.08ms native = 50.75ms overhead), which is 5u7 acceptance 3.
- A crash test proving a published CAS object is never readable at short
  bytes after the change, mutation-verified.

CONTEXT
Found while closing zerostack-5u7 for FSZero, where the identical symptom
(fixed cost per round-trip, does not scale with work) turned out to be 3
F_FULLFSYNC per plan. FSZero is now 6.07ms/read through the router. TokenZero
is the same disease in a different engine, but needs a different cure.

title: EPIC: classify all 3,465 tests against user-facing promises, then consolidate into zero-testkit and prune
description:
Three engines carry 3,465 tests across 72,890 lines of test code against
221,449 lines of source. A large fraction is not written for the user; it is
written to cover the implementation. This EPIC classifies the whole surface
against one question, moves genuinely shared behavior into a new zero-testkit
crate, and deletes what survives neither test.

THE GOVERNING QUESTION (applies to every test, no exceptions)

  Does a failure of this test correspond to a user-visible broken promise?

Not "does this cover a code path." Not unit-vs-integration. Not coverage
percentage. If the honest answer is "this proves an internal type agrees with
itself," it goes. If the answer is "without this, the user silently loses
data / gets wrong bytes / a documented command breaks," it stays no matter
how internal it looks.

MEASURED SURFACE (2026-07-25)

  engine       #[test]   test lines   src lines   ratio
  FSZero           633       17,350      22,732   0.76:1
  TokenZero        987       19,445      80,672   0.24:1
  GraphZero      1,845       36,095     118,045   0.31:1
  TOTAL          3,465       72,890     221,449

TokenZero additionally carries 108M of generated fixtures under
tests/artifacts/perf/_corpus (untracked; local disk only, not shipped).
Confirm it is reproducible on demand, then stop materializing it by default.

DUPLICATION FOUND (the concrete case for a shared crate)

The same concept is independently reimplemented per engine:

  packaging_lifecycle     FZ 7 tests / TZ 7 / GZ 7    -- three implementations
  packaging_e2e           FZ 6 / TZ 8 / GZ 4
  racc_durability_matrix  FZ 7 / GZ 8
  readme_claims           FZ 2 / GZ 1
  readme_command_audit    FZ 1 / GZ 1

These are one behavior with three sources of drift and three places to fix a
bug. They are the first migration targets.

WORKED EXAMPLES FROM THIS REPO (calibrate the classifier against these)

  KEEP  tests/crash_injection.rs (FSZero, 17 tests). Looks like paranoid
        internals. It is the only thing standing between the fsync-barrier
        removals in e63587b/d91c483/3e420b0 and silent data loss on power
        failure. Maximally user-facing.

  CUT   tests/dispatcher_unit.rs::opcode_and_operation_round_trip (FSZero).
        Asserts an internal enum agrees with itself. No user outcome changes
        if it is deleted.

PHASES (strictly ordered -- do not delete before classifying)

Phase 1 -- inventory and classify, delete nothing.
  Enumerate all 3,465 tests. For each: engine, file, name, the specific user
  promise it guards (or "none"), and keep/move/cut. Commit the inventory as a
  reviewable artifact. A test whose promise cannot be named in one sentence is
  a cut candidate by default, but record the reasoning.

Phase 2 -- enumerate the promises, independently.
  Derive each engine's user-facing contract from README claims, the CLI
  surface, the durability contract, and the MCP/CodeMode surface. This is a
  separate pass from Phase 1 and must not be back-derived from the tests, or
  it just relabels what already exists. Cross-check: a promise with no test is
  a coverage GAP worth adding; a test with no promise is a cut candidate.

Phase 3 -- build crates/zero-testkit.
  Sits alongside zero-abi / zero-ref / zero-store. Hosts the shared behavioral
  suites (packaging, README claims, durability matrix, command audit) as
  engine-parameterized cases so one definition runs against all three.
  Coordinate with zerostack-conformance-refresh-ci-30a, which owns
  conformance/ -- the testkit should FEED the conformance suite, not become a
  second one. Decide explicitly which artifacts live where.

Phase 4 -- migrate, then delete.
  Move duplicated concepts into zero-testkit; delete the per-engine copies
  only once the shared version is proven to run green against that engine.
  Then delete the Phase-1 cut list.

Phase 5 -- report.
  Final count per engine, with the promise each surviving test guards.

TARGET

Derived, not fixed. The user's estimate is 20-30 per engine and that is the
working hypothesis, but the number must fall out of the Phase-2 promise count
rather than be imposed on it. If an engine's honest promise count is 60,
forcing 30 deletes a promise's only guard -- and deletion is irreversible in a
way that bloat is not. Report the derived number against the 20-30 hypothesis
and explain any gap.

HARD CONSTRAINTS

1. The current suite is the BASELINE proving FSZero's 9 known failures (lib
   codemode accounting x2, batch_ops, cas, cas_migration x2, child_root x5)
   and TokenZero's 5 too_many_arguments clippy errors are pre-existing.
   Capture that baseline before touching anything, or lose the ability to tell
   a new break from an old one.
2. Every deletion is a separate reviewable commit naming what was removed and
   why no user promise regressed. No bulk deletion commits.
3. Re-run the full suite after each migration batch, on RCH, and diff the
   failure set against the captured baseline. New failures block the batch.
4. Do not delete a test because it is slow, awkward, or currently failing.
   Only because no user promise depends on it.

ACCEPTANCE

1. Committed inventory classifying all 3,465 tests with named promises.
2. Committed promise enumeration per engine, derived independently of Phase 1.
3. crates/zero-testkit exists, hosts the five duplicated concepts above, and
   runs green against all three engines from one definition.
4. Per-engine test count reduced to the derived target, each survivor mapped
   to a promise.
5. Failure set after the work is a subset of the captured baseline -- zero new
   failures.
6. Coverage gaps found in Phase 2 (promise with no test) are filed as beads,
   not silently ignored.

title: Cross-surface result shape is inconsistent: zero.token.shell returns .text, zero.fs.compound('read') returns .payload.ref
description:
Found live while dogfooding 2026-07-25.

zero.token.shell(cmd)               -> result.text          (string, directly usable)
zero.fs.compound('read', {...})     -> result.payload.ref   (no .text at all)
zero.graph.*                        -> unaudited, likely a third shape

and error, and guessing wrong FAILS SILENTLY: reading .text on an fs result
yields undefined -> '' with no error. That cost multiple turns this session
and produced two verification steps that falsely reported 0 bytes.

kind of cross-engine agreement.

1. Audit the result shape of every zero.* verb across all three engines and
   document the canonical shape in the hub.
2. Converge on one accessor for inline content and one for ref-ed content.
   Ref-ing out large results is correct; disagreeing about HOW is not.
3. Make the failure loud: accessing a field that does not exist on a result

title: origin/main status file goes stale after manual checkout advance: reports old rev and built:false while serving the new binary
description:
Found live 2026-07-26 while completing the dogfooding loop.

SEQUENCE:
1. Pushed 6 FSZero perf commits (d24102d -> 3e420b0).
2. Advanced the protected checkout: git fetch + reset --hard origin/main. HEAD = 3e420b0.
3. Rebuilt with the exact documented command:
     cargo build --release -p fszero-codemode --bin fszero-codemode -j 1
   Finished in 25.46s; binary mtime 22:55.
4. Ran a plan through zero_execute. It works and is fast (search 18ms).

BUT ~/.pi/agent/zerostack-origin-main/fszero.status.json still reports:
  rev:         d24102de...   (the SUPERSEDED commit)
  refreshedAt: 2026-07-26T02:49:18Z  (before the rebuild)
  built:       false          (a release binary demonstrably exists)

So the status file describes a checkout state that no longer exists. The
binary being served is correct; the metadata about it is wrong.

WHY IT MATTERS: this status file is the ONLY way a session can answer 'is my
pushed work actually live?' -- the exact question the dogfooding loop depends
on. substrates.js:396 already documents a previous incident in this same
mechanism where 'refreshedAt froze, and pushes to origin/main silently never
went live while status cheerfully reported config-override'. This is the same
failure mode surviving in a different path: the refresh is lazy and only
scheduleOriginMainRefresh writes the stamp, so a manual advance+build never
updates it.

Same family as zerostack-4aa: the mechanism works, but its self-report is
untrustworthy, so a session cannot tell a live improvement from a stale one.

ACCEPTANCE
1. Status reflects reality regardless of who advanced the checkout -- derive
   rev from the checkout (git rev-parse HEAD) and built from binary existence
   plus mtime vs rev, rather than trusting a cached stamp.
2. built:false while a current release binary exists is itself a detectable
   inconsistency; surface it rather than reporting it flatly.
3. Regression test: advance the checkout out-of-band, rebuild, and assert the
   status snapshot reports the new rev and built:true.
4. Document the supported way to force a refresh after a manual push+build.

title: Literal '~' directories in tokenzero/ and graphzero/ hold misplaced store data; store-root resolution leaves tilde unexpanded (graphzero doubly nested)
description:
Found 2026-07-25 during a cross-engine structural audit.

TokenZero and GraphZero each contain a literal directory named '~' at repo
root, holding real ZeroStack store data written to the wrong place:

  tokenzero/~/AI/TokenZero/.zerostack/graphzero/...            413 files
  graphzero/~/AI/GraphZero/~/AI/GraphZero/.zerostack/fszero/...  13 files

Note the GraphZero path is DOUBLY NESTED: ~/AI/GraphZero/~/AI/GraphZero/.
A tilde-prefixed path was resolved against a root that already had the same
unexpanded prefix, so this is not a one-off typo -- it recurred, compounding
each time. FSZero is clean, so this is a two-engine defect, not universal.

ROOT CAUSE (to confirm): a store root of the form '~/AI/<Engine>' is used
without shell expansion -- passed to a Rust fs API or a quoted shell var, where
'~' is an ordinary character. Something then created './~/AI/...' relative to
the repo. Contents include store.sqlite3, WAL files, locks, shard bins, and
session-memory, so a real engine session was reading and writing there.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS
1. Data went somewhere nobody would look. A store that silently lands in the
   wrong directory is the same class as zerostack-e3g (store corruption) --
   the engine believed it was persisting correctly.
2. It crosses engines: tokenzero/~ contains a GRAPHZERO store, graphzero/~
   contains an FSZERO store. So the bad root is being propagated between
   engines through the shared store-root resolution path.
3. That path is exactly what zerostack-sce moves into zero-store. Fix the
   resolution there, once, or all three engines keep their own version of it.
   This is a concrete argument for the ee2/sce consolidation.

DELIVERABLES
1. Find the writer. Grep for '~' in store-root construction across both
   engines; check ZEROSTACK_/FSZERO_ROOT/GZ_REPO_ROOT/TOKENZERO_ROOT env
   handling and any script passing a quoted '~/...'.
2. Fix in the shared store-root resolver (coordinate with sce): either expand
   '~' explicitly, or REJECT a leading '~' with a clear error. Never create a
   literal '~' directory.
3. Regression test: resolving '~/foo' as a store root either yields $HOME/foo
   or errors -- and never produces a directory named '~'.
4. Clean up: confirm the 426 files are recoverable/duplicated elsewhere, then
   delete both trees. Do not delete before confirming nothing unique lives
   there.
5. Add a repo-hygiene check that fails if a path component equal to '~' appears
   anywhere in the working tree.

title: TRACKER: structural convergence across the three engines (layout, gates, shared-crate adoption, store-root, tests)
description:
The owner's observation, measured 2026-07-25: the three engines are not three
instances of one design. They are three different designs, and that difference
is why the same bug must be fixed three times.

MEASURED LAYOUT DIVERGENCE

  engine     top-level src/   crates/   root Cargo.toml
  FSZero     YES, 103 files       3      is itself a package (lib)
  TokenZero  none                 9      pure virtual workspace
  GraphZero  none                12      pure virtual workspace

FSZero is a monolith with 103 files at src/ that grew 3 satellite crates.
TokenZero and GraphZero are proper workspaces. Consequences already observed:

- A naive audit grepping <repo>/src returns ZERO for TokenZero and GraphZero
  and gives a false 'no duplication' reading. This happened during the audit
  that produced this bead -- the first pass concluded blake3/rusqlite/CAS were
  FSZero-only, which is wrong. Tooling that assumes one layout silently
  mis-measures two of three engines.
- 'Where does X live?' has three different answers, so cross-engine work costs
  a discovery step every time.

WHAT IS ALREADY CONSISTENT (do not churn these)
  edition 2024 + nightly toolchain: all three agree.
  zero-abi + zero-ref: adopted by all three.
So convergence is achievable; it has already happened twice.

WHAT IS INCONSISTENT (the actual backlog)
1. Layout: monolithic src/ vs workspace-of-crates (above).
2. zero-store adoption: GraphZero only. FSZero and TokenZero keep private CAS
   copies -- see ee2, which now carries the measured symbol-level evidence.
3. Store-root resolution: divergent enough that two engines wrote real store
   data into a literal '~' directory (zerostack-tilde-store-root-2r6), one of
   them doubly nested.
4. Gates: TokenZero enforces fmt AND clippy; FSZero enforces neither. So the
   same code is acceptable in one repo and rejected in another.
5. Test organization: three independent implementations of packaging_lifecycle
